paragraphs.text: On a still summer evening, a cyclist leaving the centre of a large city for the open fields beyond may notice the air growing noticeably cooler with every kilometre. The effect is not imagined. Meteorologists have long recorded that built-up areas are warmer than the land around them, a pattern known as the urban heat island. The size of the gap varies with the city and the weather, but it is often a few degrees and can, on calm, clear nights, exceed ten. Surprisingly, the contrast is usually greatest after dark rather than in the heat of the afternoon. During the day, sunshine warms town and countryside alike; it is at night, when fields cool quickly but streets go on releasing the warmth they have stored, that the difference becomes most obvious.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Several features of the built environment combine to produce this effect. The first is the choice of materials. Asphalt, brick and concrete absorb a large share of the sunlight that falls on them and hold that energy for hours, behaving much like the stones of a storage heater. The second is the absence of plants. In the countryside, a good deal of the sun's energy is spent evaporating water from soil and leaves, a process that cools the surroundings in the same way that sweat cools the skin; in a city where rain runs quickly into drains, far less energy is used up in this way. The shape of the city matters too. Tall buildings lining narrow streets form what climate scientists call 'urban canyons', which block cooling breezes and prevent heat from escaping to the open sky at night. Finally, cities generate heat of their own, from engines, factories and, ironically, the air-conditioning units that push warm air out of buildings and into the street.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The consequences go well beyond discomfort. During heatwaves, death rates rise sharply in cities, and doctors point out that the warm nights may be as dangerous as the hot days, because the body never gets the chance to recover. Elderly people living alone, and those with heart or lung conditions, are at particular risk. Higher temperatures also raise the demand for electricity as residents switch on fans and air conditioners, which in turn can strain power networks at exactly the moment they are most needed. Where that electricity comes from burning fossil fuels, the extra demand adds to the emissions that are warming the planet as a whole. Heat even affects the air people breathe: warm, sunny conditions speed up the chemical reactions that form ground-level ozone, a pollutant that irritates the lungs.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Nor is the burden shared equally. When a team led by the geographer Marta Venn mapped surface temperatures across one large port city using satellite images, they found differences of up to seven degrees between neighbourhoods only a few kilometres apart. The hottest districts were, almost without exception, the poorest, with densely packed housing, few parks and wide roads offering little shade. Wealthier suburbs, by contrast, were lined with mature trees and private gardens. Venn argues that this pattern is no accident, since decisions about where to plant trees, build highways or locate industry have often been made with little regard for the people living nearby. Residents of the hottest areas are also the least likely to own air conditioning or to be able to afford running it.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Cities have begun to fight back, and the simplest measures involve changing the colour of surfaces. Roofs coated with pale, reflective paint can stay many degrees cooler than dark ones on a sunny day, lowering the temperature of the rooms beneath them as well as of the surrounding air. Some authorities are experimenting with lighter-coloured paving for the same reason. Vegetation offers a second approach. Trees shade streets and walls while also releasing water vapour through their leaves, and parks can form pockets of cooler air that spread into neighbouring blocks. In a three-year trial, the urban ecologist Tomas Reiner compared streets that had received new tree planting with similar streets that had not, and recorded afternoon air temperatures up to two degrees lower beneath the young canopy. Green roofs, covered with low-growing plants, also help, though Reiner found their effect at street level to be modest, since most of the cooling stays on the rooftop.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: None of these solutions is perfect. Reflective pavements can bounce sunlight back onto pedestrians and the walls of nearby buildings, so that people walking on them may actually feel hotter. Trees need water, space for their roots and years of care before they provide meaningful shade, and in dry regions irrigating them may compete with other needs. For these reasons, most specialists now favour a mixture of measures chosen to suit local conditions rather than a single remedy. The heat island will not disappear while cities remain dense collections of stone and steel, but with careful planning its worst effects can be softened. As global temperatures continue to rise, that task is likely to become one of the most pressing challenges facing those who design and run the world's cities.
paragraphs.label: F

section.text:
The Hidden Heat of Cities

A. On a still summer evening, a cyclist leaving the centre of a large city for the open fields beyond may notice the air growing noticeably cooler with every kilometre. The effect is not imagined. Meteorologists have long recorded that built-up areas are warmer than the land around them, a pattern known as the urban heat island. The size of the gap varies with the city and the weather, but it is often a few degrees and can, on calm, clear nights, exceed ten. Surprisingly, the contrast is usually greatest after dark rather than in the heat of the afternoon. During the day, sunshine warms town and countryside alike; it is at night, when fields cool quickly but streets go on releasing the warmth they have stored, that the difference becomes most obvious.

B. Several features of the built environment combine to produce this effect. The first is the choice of materials. Asphalt, brick and concrete absorb a large share of the sunlight that falls on them and hold that energy for hours, behaving much like the stones of a storage heater. The second is the absence of plants. In the countryside, a good deal of the sun's energy is spent evaporating water from soil and leaves, a process that cools the surroundings in the same way that sweat cools the skin; in a city where rain runs quickly into drains, far less energy is used up in this way. The shape of the city matters too. Tall buildings lining narrow streets form what climate scientists call 'urban canyons', which block cooling breezes and prevent heat from escaping to the open sky at night. Finally, cities generate heat of their own, from engines, factories and, ironically, the air-conditioning units that push warm air out of buildings and into the street.

C. The consequences go well beyond discomfort. During heatwaves, death rates rise sharply in cities, and doctors point out that the warm nights may be as dangerous as the hot days, because the body never gets the chance to recover. Elderly people living alone, and those with heart or lung conditions, are at particular risk. Higher temperatures also raise the demand for electricity as residents switch on fans and air conditioners, which in turn can strain power networks at exactly the moment they are most needed. Where that electricity comes from burning fossil fuels, the extra demand adds to the emissions that are warming the planet as a whole. Heat even affects the air people breathe: warm, sunny conditions speed up the chemical reactions that form ground-level ozone, a pollutant that irritates the lungs.

D. Nor is the burden shared equally. When a team led by the geographer Marta Venn mapped surface temperatures across one large port city using satellite images, they found differences of up to seven degrees between neighbourhoods only a few kilometres apart. The hottest districts were, almost without exception, the poorest, with densely packed housing, few parks and wide roads offering little shade. Wealthier suburbs, by contrast, were lined with mature trees and private gardens. Venn argues that this pattern is no accident, since decisions about where to plant trees, build highways or locate industry have often been made with little regard for the people living nearby. Residents of the hottest areas are also the least likely to own air conditioning or to be able to afford running it.

E. Cities have begun to fight back, and the simplest measures involve changing the colour of surfaces. Roofs coated with pale, reflective paint can stay many degrees cooler than dark ones on a sunny day, lowering the temperature of the rooms beneath them as well as of the surrounding air. Some authorities are experimenting with lighter-coloured paving for the same reason. Vegetation offers a second approach. Trees shade streets and walls while also releasing water vapour through their leaves, and parks can form pockets of cooler air that spread into neighbouring blocks. In a three-year trial, the urban ecologist Tomas Reiner compared streets that had received new tree planting with similar streets that had not, and recorded afternoon air temperatures up to two degrees lower beneath the young canopy. Green roofs, covered with low-growing plants, also help, though Reiner found their effect at street level to be modest, since most of the cooling stays on the rooftop.

F. None of these solutions is perfect. Reflective pavements can bounce sunlight back onto pedestrians and the walls of nearby buildings, so that people walking on them may actually feel hotter. Trees need water, space for their roots and years of care before they provide meaningful shade, and in dry regions irrigating them may compete with other needs. For these reasons, most specialists now favour a mixture of measures chosen to suit local conditions rather than a single remedy. The heat island will not disappear while cities remain dense collections of stone and steel, but with careful planning its worst effects can be softened. As global temperatures continue to rise, that task is likely to become one of the most pressing challenges facing those who design and run the world's cities.

explanation.en: Paragraph C says warm nights may be as dangerous as hot days because the body never gets the chance to recover. Ozone and power networks are mentioned, but not as reasons why nights are dangerous.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C сказано, что тёплые ночи могут быть так же опасны, как жаркие дни, потому что организм так и не получает возможности восстановиться. Озон и электросети упоминаются, но не как причины того, что ночи опасны.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C сказано, що теплі ночі можуть бути так само небезпечними, як спекотні дні, бо організм так і не отримує змоги відновитися. Озон і електромережі згадано, але не як причини того, що ночі небезпечні.

options.text: They could be removed by providing air conditioning in poorer districts.

questions.prompt: What does Marta Venn believe about the temperature differences her team found?
questions.evidence: decisions about where to plant trees, build highways or locate industry have often been made with little regard for the people living nearby

explanation.en: In paragraph D, Venn says the pattern is 'no accident' because past decisions paid little attention to nearby residents. The port is mentioned only to describe the city.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D Венн говорит, что такая картина — 'no accident', потому что при принятии прежних решений мало считались с местными жителями. Порт упоминается лишь для описания города.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D Венн каже, що така картина — 'no accident', бо під час ухвалення попередніх рішень мало зважали на місцевих мешканців. Порт згадано лише для опису міста.
